cards.q: What is the three-tier / hierarchical model?
cards.a: It layers the LAN as Core, Distribution, and Access. This is Cisco's classic campus framework where each layer has a distinct role, making the network scalable, predictable, and easy to tune. It is used for large campuses, multi-building sites, and enterprise cores where a two-tier collapsed core is too big.

cards.q: What does each layer in the three-tier model do?
cards.a: Access provides endpoint connectivity: ports, VLAN assignment, PoE, port security/802.1X, and QoS trust on endpoints. Distribution handles policy, routing, and aggregation: inter-VLAN routing, ACLs/firewalling, QoS marking, default gateways (HSRP/VRRP), and summarization. Core is the fast L3 transport backbone with no policy, for maximum speed and redundancy.

cards.q: What are the key rules of the three-tier layers?
cards.a: Core is fast and dumb — never attach users or policy to it. Distribution is the smart layer, being the aggregation and policy point or 'routing brain.' Access is simple and cheap, kept shallow while the distribution holds the logic.

cards.q: How does traffic flow and summarization work in a three-tier design?
cards.a: North-south flows traverse access-to-distribution-to-core (e.g., to servers or WAN). Distribution performs summarization of VLANs into summary routes toward the core, keeping core tables small and convergence fast. Redundancy is everywhere with dual uplinks from access to both distribution switches and from the distribution pair to the core pair.

cards.q: What are the variants and scaling options of the three-tier model?
cards.a: Small sites use collapsed core (two-tier). Large sites split the distribution per building, with each pair owning its VLANs/subnets and the core interconnecting them. In modern data centers, spine-leaf replaces the rigid 3-tier, but the access/dist/core logic still underpins design questions.

cards.q: How is redundancy handled in a three-tier design (STP and FHRP)?
cards.a: L2 loops from dual uplinks are handled by MST/RPVST+. Distribution pairs run first-hop redundancy (HSRP/VRRP) so hosts always have a gateway. Core failure triggers routing protocols to converge, since distribution-to-core is usually routed.

cards.q: What commands set up gateway redundancy and summarization in a three-tier design?
cards.a: On the distribution switch, configure 'interface Vlan10' with 'ip address 10.1.10.1 255.255.255.0', 'standby 10 ip 10.1.10.254', and 'standby 10 priority 120' for the active/backup pair. Summarize toward the core with 'router ospf 1' and 'summary-address 10.1.0.0 255.255.252.0'. The core is pure L3 with just 'ip address 10.0.0.1 255.255.255.252' and no VLANs/policy.

cards.q: What is the number one three-tier exam trap, and what is the correct answer?
cards.a: The trap is putting policy in the core. The correct answer is 'core = transport, distribution = policy.'

cards.q: Where is the best place for the default gateway in a three-tier design?
cards.a: At the distribution layer, not at access or core.

cards.q: Must access switches in a three-tier design route?
cards.a: No. Access switches may be L2 (common) — do not insist they must route.

cards.q: Where does Spanning Tree belong in the three-tier model?
cards.a: STP belongs to the L2 access/distribution spans; the routed core has none.

cards.q: Map the exam synonyms: 'collapsed core' and 'hierarchical' correspond to what tier counts?
In the three-tier Quick Review, summarize each layer's responsibility and watch-list.
cards.a: Access handles ports, VLANs, PoE, edge security — keep simple. Distribution does routing, policy, gateways, summarization — the smart layer. Core is the fast L3 backbone — no policy. Redundancy uses dual uplinks everywhere with HSRP/VRRP and STP. Sizing favors three-tier for large campuses; small sites use collapsed core.
